title: One hand
hookLine: Hakuin's koan: you know the sound of two hands; what is the sound of one
carry: listen for what's under the noise
last: ORDINARY MIND — NOTHING USELESS CLINGS TO THE MIND.

lines: A PUNCH LINE AT A PARTY.
ONE HAND WAVED IN THE AIR.
A REAL HOME, A REAL AUTHOR.
cards: You've heard it, probably in a cartoon, or from a friend being clever at a party: what's the sound of one hand clapping? It's become a punch line, shorthand for a question so deep it's silly.
Somebody waves one hand in the air, and everybody laughs.

But the question has a real home and a real author: a Japanese monk who lived in a small, poor temple at the foot of Mount Fuji, painted wild ink pictures, and nearly broke his own health with practice when he was young.

teach.b: His name was Hakuin Ekaku, and he lived from 1686 to 1769. He's remembered as the teacher who revived Rinzai Zen in Japan when it had grown sleepy; almost every Rinzai teacher in Japan today traces their line through him.
For years Hakuin gave his students mu, Zhaozhou's dog, as their first koan. Then, late in life, he started giving them a question of his own.
In a letter written in his late sixties, he explains it roughly like this: clap two hands together and there's a sound. What is the sound of one hand?
He wrote that this question raised the great doubt in students more easily than mu. Notice what it does to you. The thinking mind reaches for an answer and finds nothing to grab.
One hand makes no sound; any fool knows that. So what is he asking?
The koan pushes attention toward listening itself, toward what's here before any sound, the silence every sound comes out of and goes back into.
Students work with it for months, sometimes years, and teachers follow up with more questions: hear the sound of one hand from the soles of your feet, or stop the sound of one hand.
Hakuin never meant it as a joke, but he had a big sense of humor; his paintings of monks and gods are full of it. He'd probably laugh at the party version too. Then he'd ask you to listen.

how: In Japanese Rinzai Zen, Hakuin's 'sound of one hand' is one of the first koans a teacher may assign, often alongside or instead of mu, followed by a series of checking questions in private interviews.

games.q: you're a student of Hakuin. he asks: what is the sound of one hand? what do you bring to him?
o: a clever explanation of why one hand makes no sound.
a direct response from your own listening, after sitting with it.
games.why: like all koans, it's met directly, not explained; teachers then test it with further questions.

practice: First, just listen to whatever sounds are here: traffic, a fan, a bird, your own breath. Then notice the silence those sounds rise out of and fall back into, and rest there.
If you like, lift one hand a little and ask: what is the sound of this? Don't answer; just listen.
